# 2 Kings 16 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 1 — “In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham became king of Judah.”

Ahaz is the 12th king of Judah (of 20 total). This chronological note ties his accession to events in the northern kingdom, showing how intertwined the two kingdoms' histories had become. Ahaz inherited the throne from his godly father Jotham at a time of mounting political tension — Israel and Aram (Syria) were pressuring Judah to join an anti-Assyrian alliance. What looks like a routine chronological note actually introduces a dramatic turning point in Judah's spiritual and national life. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-16-commentary)

Gill notes that Jotham began in Pekah's second year and reigned sixteen years, so his last year fell toward the end of Pekah's seventeenth, reconciling the chronology. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/16.htm)

---

## v. 2 — “Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king… he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God, as his father David had done.”

**Age problem:** Both the Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott note a well-known difficulty: if Ahaz was 20 at accession, he would have been only ~10 when his son Hezekiah was born (since Hezekiah was 25 when he succeeded Ahaz 16 years later — 2 Kings 18:2). Several ancient witnesses (LXX, Syriac, some Hebrew MSS) read “twenty-five,” which is preferred by many scholars. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

**Traditional reading:** Ahaz is described in starkly negative terms. Guzik calls him “perhaps the worst king of Judah.” Unlike many predecessors who fell short only on the high-places issue, Ahaz is simply said to have done nothing right. He had every advantage — a godly father (Jotham) and the example of David — yet rejected them all. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

Gill observes: “grace is neither propagated by blood, nor obtained through the force of education.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/16.htm)

Precept Austin expands: “Ahaz's life proves there is no such thing as 'inherited faith,' for he was nothing like his father Jotham. Having godly lineage does not make anyone godly!” The phrase “his God” is noted to be covenantal language — Ahaz belonged to the covenant people by birth, but there is no evidence he ever entered a personal relationship with God. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-16-commentary)

**Reformed/Baptist perspective (Piper, Desiring God):** John Piper uses Ahaz as a sobering example that parents cannot guarantee a child's godliness. Jotham was a faithful father, yet Ahaz “rejected all of it — a slave to sin, a son of disobedience, a child of wrath.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/you-cannot-guarantee-your-childs-godliness)

---

## v. 3 — “Instead, he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and even sacrificed his son in the fire…”

**Traditional reading:** Ahaz adopted the worst practices of the northern kingdom. Guzik notes this is “the first instance where Judah imitates Israel's apostasy” (citing Wiseman). The phrase “made his son pass through the fire” describes participation in Molech worship. Guzik details the horrific rite: a metal statue was heated red-hot, a living infant was placed on its outstretched hands, and drums drowned out the child's screams until death. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

Ellicott explains that the expression “to make to pass through the fire to Molech” (Leviticus 18:21) may have originated in the idea that the burning was a passage to union with the deity after the dross of the flesh was purged — or it may be a euphemism. He notes Ahaz was the first Israelite king to offer such a sacrifice, probably as “a last desperate resource against the oppression of his northern enemies.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

The Pulpit Commentary provides extensive detail from classical sources (Diodorus Siculus, Plutarch) describing the Carthaginian (Phoenician) version of the rite: an image of Saturn/Molech with a bull's head and outstretched arms, heated glowing hot; children rolled from the arms into a fiery lap below. Mothers stood by without tears, and the noise of flutes and drums drowned out cries. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

Precept Austin notes that 2 Chronicles 28:3 says Ahaz “burnt his children in the fire” — plural — suggesting he sacrificed more than one son. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-16-commentary)

**Piper (Baptist/Reformed):** Piper calls these “ceremonial abortions after he had held the babies in his arms” — a devastating picture of rejecting God's fatherhood. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/you-cannot-guarantee-your-childs-godliness)

---

## v. 4 — “And he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.”

**Traditional reading:** Unlike earlier kings of Judah who merely tolerated high-place worship, Ahaz personally participated in it — “which no other king appears to have done” (Pulpit Commentary). That Ahaz's example stimulated the cult is suggested by the fact that Hezekiah later abolished the high places. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

Ellicott distinguishes “high places” (*bâmâh*) from “hills” — two different Hebrew prepositions are used. A *bâmâh* was a local sanctuary; a sacred pillar or altar might be called a *bâmâh*. “Under every green tree” refers to thick-foliaged, shadow-yielding trees (oaks, poplars, teil trees — cf. Hosea 4:13). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

Precept Austin notes: “The Holy Spirit uses three locations to show how thoroughly Ahaz abandoned the worship of Yahweh. Ahaz replaced God's appointed worship with a veritable smorgasbord of pagan devotion.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-16-commentary)

---

## v. 5 — “Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to wage war against Jerusalem. They besieged Ahaz but could not overcome him.”

**Traditional reading:** This is the Syro-Ephraimite War, also described in Isaiah 7. Pekah and Rezin formed an anti-Assyrian coalition and attacked Judah because Ahaz refused to join. Their goal, per Isaiah 7:6, was to dethrone Ahaz and install a puppet ruler (“the son of Tabeal”). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

The allies could not storm Jerusalem because Uzziah and Jotham had strongly fortified it (2 Chronicles 26:9; 27:3). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

Guzik notes that God did not permit this “Satanic plot against the Messianic dynasty of David” to succeed. Through Isaiah, God assured Ahaz that the two kings were merely “burnt-out smoking sticks” (Isaiah 7:4) who would not ultimately prevail. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that Judah suffered terrible losses in this war — 2 Chronicles 28:5-8 records 120,000 Judean soldiers killed and 200,000 civilians taken captive. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

---

## v. 6 — “At that time Rezin king of Aram recovered Elath for Aram, drove out the men of Judah, and sent the Edomites into Elath, where they live to this day.”

**Text-critical issue:** This verse contains a well-known textual problem. The Hebrew reads “Aram” (Syria), but many scholars argue the original reading was “Edom” (the Hebrew letters for *Aram* and *Edom* are easily confused — *dalet* vs. *resh*). Ellicott notes the Hebrew margin, many MSS, the LXX, and Vulgate read “Edomites” for “Syrians.” If so, Rezin emancipated the Edomites from Judah's yoke (imposed by Uzziah, 2 Kings 14:22) to win their support against Judah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

The Pulpit Commentary similarly argues that Rezin could not have held a place as remote as Damascus from Elath; it makes more sense that he “recovered” Elath *for Edom*. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

Guzik takes the reading as is: Rezin captured Elath and the Edomites then moved in permanently (“to this day”). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

---

## v. 7 — “So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, 'I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me…'”

**Traditional reading:** This is the pivotal spiritual failure of Ahaz. Instead of trusting God — who through Isaiah had offered him a sign (Isaiah 7:10-12) — Ahaz appealed to Assyria. Guzik says: “Ahaz surrendered to one enemy in order to defeat another. He refused to trust in the God of Israel and instead submitted himself and his kingdom to an enemy of Israel.” The address “I am your servant and your son” is formal vassal language — Ahaz placed Judah under Assyrian suzerainty. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

Precept Austin highlights the irony: “Ahaz's plea for salvation should have been spoken to Yahweh, the Rock of our salvation, but instead was spoken to the godless pagan king Tiglath-pileser.” The Hebrew word for “deliver” here (*yasha*) is the same root as the name “Jesus.” “The heir of the coming Messiah was seeking salvation from a pagan empire.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-16-commentary)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that Ahaz was young and weak, surrounded by worldly advisors who considered Isaiah a fanatic and trusted only in human policy. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

---

## v. 8 — “Ahaz also took the silver and gold found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's palace, and he sent it as a gift to the king of Assyria.”

Guzik observes that Ahaz essentially made Judah a subject kingdom, sacrificing its independence. He asks: “We can only wonder what blessing might have come if Ahaz would have surrendered and sacrificed to the LORD with the same energy and whole heart that he surrendered to the Assyrian king.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that temple treasures had previously been used to buy off hostile foreign foes (1 Kings 14:26; 2 Kings 12:18), but now they were used to purchase an alliance — a further degradation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

---

## v. 9 — “So the king of Assyria responded to him, marched up to Damascus, and captured it. He took its people to Kir as captives and put Rezin to death.”

Tiglath-pileser III's annals confirm this campaign. Ellicott notes the Eponym-list shows Tiglath-pileser marched against Damascus for two successive years (733 and 732 BC). The city fell after a two-year siege. The Assyrian king's inscription records: “Damascus, his city, I besieged, and like a caged bird I enclosed him.” Sir H. Rawlinson found a tablet (since lost) recording Rezin's death. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that Tiglath-pileser began the system of mass deportation, removing over 30,000 captives according to his fragmentary annals — a precedent followed by later Assyrian kings. The location of “Kir” is uncertain despite many proposals. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

---

## vv. 10-11 — “Then King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser… On seeing the altar in Damascus, King Ahaz sent Uriah the priest a model of the altar… And Uriah the priest built the altar…”

**Traditional reading:** This was an official act of submission — Ahaz went to pay homage to his new overlord. Guzik notes it was unusual for Judah's kings to make official visits to other kingdoms; they generally stayed within the Promised Land. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

The Pulpit Commentary argues the altar Ahaz saw was an Assyrian altar, not a Syrian one. Assyrian kings carried altars with them on campaign and sometimes required conquered peoples to set them up. Ahaz was likely complying with Tiglath-pileser's requirements or volunteering the act to please his suzerain. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

Guzik notes 2 Chronicles 28:23 explains Ahaz's thinking: “Because the gods of the kings of Syria help them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me.” He calls this a warning for churches that “put their trust in the tools, techniques, and principles of worldly success.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

**Uriah's complicity:** Uriah the high priest complied eagerly and without recorded protest. Guzik notes this is likely the same “faithful witness” Uriah of Isaiah 8:2, suggesting he was a good man who later compromised. Ellicott similarly observes that Isaiah's “faithful witness” could be a reference to his official reliability, not his character. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

The Pulpit Commentary contrasts Uriah unfavorably with the bold high priest Azariah who resisted King Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:17): “Urijah was a man of a weaker fiber, and does not seem to have thought even of remonstrance, much less of resistance.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

---

## v. 12 — “When the king came back from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached it and presented offerings on it.”

Ellicott notes that all ancient versions (except the Targum) render this as “went up thereon” — meaning Ahaz personally ascended the altar to officiate, like Uzziah before him (1 Kings 12:32-33). He thus usurped the priestly function of sacrifice, disregarding Numbers 18:7. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

Guzik contrasts this with his grandfather Uzziah: “Uzziah for so doing was smitten with leprosy; but Ahaz of a far worse disease, an incurable hardness of heart” (quoting Trapp). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

---

## v. 13 — “He offered his burnt offering and his grain offering, poured out his drink offering, and sprinkled the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.”

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott says this describes a thank-offering for deliverance from his enemies. From the Kings account alone, it appears Ahaz may have offered these to Yahweh — but 2 Chronicles 28:23 clarifies that he also sacrificed to the gods of Damascus. Many in Ahaz's time thought the worship of Yahweh was not incompatible with the cult of foreign deities. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

Guzik says Ahaz “served as a priest at the altar of his own design. Since he created his own place of worship, it also made sense that he would disregard God's command that a king must not serve as a priest.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

---

## v. 14 — “He also took the bronze altar that stood before the LORD… and he put it on the north side of the new altar.”

**Traditional reading:** The old bronze altar of Solomon originally stood directly before the temple porch. Uriah, having no specific instructions, had placed the new altar in front of the old one. Ahaz was dissatisfied because the old altar still appeared to have precedence. Ellicott explains: “Ahaz, not satisfied with this arrangement, which appeared to confer a kind of precedence on the old altar, drew it back again, and fixed it on the north side of his new altar.” Thus the new pagan altar now occupied the position of prominence. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

Guzik says: “The plain brazen altar seems to have offended his aesthetic eye; so it was relegated to a place of relative obscurity on the north side of his own foreign substitute” (quoting Knapp). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

---

## v. 15 — “Then King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, 'Offer on the great altar the morning burnt offering… But I will use the bronze altar to seek guidance.'”

The “great altar” means the new Syrian-style altar (like “the high altar”). Ahaz commanded that all official sacrifices — daily national sacrifices, royal offerings, and private offerings — be made on the new altar. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

**The phrase “the bronze altar shall be for me to inquire by”** is debated. Ellicott lists several interpretations: Rashi understood it as “for consulting God”; Keil rendered it “I will think about what to do with it”; others suggest “it shall be for me to look at” (as an ornamental piece), or that the old altar of sacrifice would become an altar of prayer. The meaning is uncertain. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

Gill's Exposition suggests Ahaz reserved the bronze altar for himself to seek divine guidance (possibly by augury), while all public worship was transferred to the new altar. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/16.htm)

---

## v. 17 — “King Ahaz also cut off the frames of the movable stands and removed the bronze basin from each of them. He took down the Sea from the bronze oxen that were under it and put it on a stone base.”

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott provides the interpretive key: these actions were not wanton malice but “dire necessity.” Ahaz had to provide further tribute to Assyria, having exhausted his first payment. He stripped the temple of its ornamental bronze-work to send as a present. Professor Robertson Smith says: “Ahaz, whose treasures had been exhausted by his first tribute, was soon driven by the repeated demands of his masters to strip the Temple even of its ancient bronze-work and other fixed ornaments.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

Gill notes the ten lavers with their engraved bronze bases (see 1 Kings 7:27-28) had borders featuring lions, oxen, and cherubim. Ahaz cut these off, either to deface them in contempt or to convert the brass to other uses. The bronze oxen supporting the great Sea were later carried off by the Babylonians (Jeremiah 52:20). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/16.htm)

Guzik offers an alternative view: this was not just about tribute — Ahaz was “de-emphasizing their importance in the worship services,” actively working to discourage true worship of Yahweh. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

---

## v. 18 — “And on account of the king of Assyria, he removed the Sabbath canopy they had built in the temple and closed the royal entryway outside the house of the LORD.”

**Traditional reading:** The “covert for the Sabbath” (*mûsak* in the Hebrew margin) is a very obscure expression. Ellicott says the best interpretation is “the covered hall (or stand) set apart for the use of the king and his attendants when he visited the Temple on holy days.” It is not mentioned anywhere else. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

Gill offers multiple possibilities: it may have been a covered place for the people to sit under to hear the law explained, or for the priests of the outgoing course to remain until evening, or a rich canopy for the king while attending temple service. The “king's entry” was the direct passage from the palace to the temple — Ahaz either closed it or altered its route. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/16.htm)

The phrase “on account of the king of Assyria” is understood variously: Gill says Ahaz wanted to gratify his overlord by showing he had abandoned Yahweh-worship and would cleave to the gods of Damascus; or he feared the Assyrian king might use the passage to seize temple treasures or find Ahaz hiding there. Ellicott says Ahaz could not appear before Tiglath-pileser without a present, so he stripped these features for their valuable materials. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

Guzik adds a symbolic reading: “He destroyed the link that his father Jotham made between the palace and the temple, and this was an illustration of his destroyed relationship with God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

---

## v. 19 — “As for the rest of the acts of Ahaz, along with his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?”

The standard closing formula. Gill notes that some of Ahaz's other acts are preserved in the canonical book of 2 Chronicles 28, and the rest were probably in the royal annals of Judah, now lost. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/16.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary notes the formula here is “wholly colorless” — the writer adds no praise and no further condemnation, simply recording the fact. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

---

## v. 20 — “And Ahaz rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David, and his son Hezekiah reigned in his place.”

**Traditional reading:** Though Ahaz was buried in Jerusalem, 2 Chronicles 28:27 specifies he was *not* placed in the tombs of the kings — a mark of dishonor. Gill: “But not in the sepulchres of the kings of Israel, as David and Solomon, he being such a wicked prince.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/16.htm)

Guzik notes the stark contrast: Ahaz died at 36, and his son Hezekiah — one of Judah's greatest kings — reversed all his father's corruptions. Guzik applies this to modern readers: Ahaz was like a 21st-century church leader — artistic, impressed with technology, in love with innovation, seemingly “nice,” yet possessing no actual relationship with God. “Ahaz had every advantage… yet lacked the one thing that mattered: an actual relationship with God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

Precept Austin quotes Charles Swindoll: “We usually expect that godly parents are going to bring up godly children. But that isn't always the case… Each of us is dependent on God for His grace.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-16-commentary)

---

## Traditions and Distinctive Readings

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik's Pentecostal background is evident in his emphasis on personal relationship with God over mere religious activity, and his application about churches importing “worldly methods” into worship (the “gods of Damascus”). His pastoral tone stresses the heart over externals. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-16/)

### Reformed / Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper)
Piper draws the lesson of divine sovereignty in salvation: Ahaz had a godly father (Jotham), the prophets Isaiah and Micah, and God's protection — yet he rejected God. This demonstrates that “grace is neither propagated by blood, nor obtained through the force of education.” Piper sees Ahaz's child sacrifice as “ceremonial abortions” and a warning about pragmatism — sacrificing to whatever “works.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/you-cannot-guarantee-your-childs-godliness; https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/pastors-pragmatism-pleasure-and-pride)

### Anglican (Ellicott's Commentary)
Ellicott (1878) provides meticulous textual and historical notes. He reads the temple-stripping (vv. 17-18) as driven by financial necessity (tribute to Assyria), not merely wanton destruction. His notes on the LXX variant for Ahaz's age (25 vs. 20) and the Edom/Aram textual problem in v. 6 represent standard Anglican scholarly care. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-16.html)

### Older Baptist (Gill's Exposition, 1746–63)
Gill provides particularly detailed notes on the temple furnishings and possible meanings of obscure phrases. He suggests multiple possibilities for the “Sabbath covert” and the “king's entry,” showing familiarity with rabbinic sources. His theological comment that Ahaz, though wicked, was still in the Davidic line and “God had a purpose for Judah” reflects a covenantal Baptist perspective. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/16.htm)

### Pulpit Commentary (1880, broader Protestant / Reformed Anglican)
The Pulpit Commentary provides the most thorough historical background, including classical sources (Diodorus Siculus, Plutarch) on Molech worship, and extensive Assyrian historical correlations. It emphasizes Ahaz as the worst king of Judah to that point. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-16.html)

---

The NET Bible notes (netbible.org) and bibleodyssey.org would provide modern scholarly perspectives but were similarly not reached.
